extracted.intended_audience: students and coaches preparing for mathematical olympiads / contest problem solvers (high-school to early undergraduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of combinatorics and number-theory problem statements and worked solutions illustrating standard contest techniques (double counting, recurrences, modular obstructions, Hall's marriage lemma, binary reasoning, parametrizations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Count twice / double counting
rubrics_metrics.description: Count the elements (or weight/sum) of a set in two different ways to obtain an identity or contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count a combinatorial set by two viewpoints (e.g., choose committee with chairman: count by choosing members then chairman vs choosing chairman first gives C(n,k)k = nC(n-1,k-1)); arrange terms into arrays and sum by rows vs columns to derive contradictions or bounds (used for sequences with sums of consecutive terms negative/positive). Examples: Problems 3.19, 3.20 (7×11 table), 3.21 (counting fractions to derive sum_{d|n} phi(d)=n), 3.22–3.33. Anti-pattern: counting only one way or mixing incompatible partitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange into table and sum by rows/columns
rubrics_metrics.description: Place sequence or multiset elements into a rectangular array so that summing by rows vs by columns yields different decompositions of the same total.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to compare overlaps of sliding windows or to turn local constraints into global contradictions (e.g., sums of every 7 consecutive negative vs every 11 consecutive positive, arrange first 17 terms into 7×11 table and sum rows vs columns). Examples: Problem 3.20. Guidance: choose table dimensions to reflect the local window sizes; count each entry exactly once in both directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modular arithmetic / residues to rule out integer solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze congruence classes (residues) of powers or expressions modulo an appropriate modulus to show that an equation cannot hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute possible residues of cubes, fourth powers, etc., modulo a chosen base and show the target congruence is impossible (e.g., cubes mod 9 give {0,±1} so x^3+y^3+z^3 cannot be 4 mod 9 ⇒ no solution for 2002; cubes mod 7 or fourth powers mod 13 used similarly). Examples: Problems 3.59–3.61 and many 'no solutions' problems. Choose modulus that distinguishes possible residues of the relevant powers. Anti-pattern: picking modulus that gives too many residues to be informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence relations: invariants and induction to prove integrality/positivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform recurrences to invariant forms or rational-constant forms, then use induction to prove all terms have desired arithmetic properties (integers, positivity, perfect squares, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for conserved ratios or linear relations (e.g., show (a_{n+1}+a_{n-1})/a_n is constant, reduce to linear recurrence an+1 = k an − an−1 and use induction). Use substitution, telescoping, or strong induction. Examples: Problems 3.34–3.36, 3.40–3.46, 3.89–3.91. Anti-pattern: attempting termwise divisibility without establishing a stable invariant or base-case induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct infinite families via parametrization or linear recurrences
rubrics_metrics.description: Given one nontrivial solution, produce an infinite family using parametrizations (e.g., Pythagorean parameterization) or linear transformations/recurrences that map solutions to solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard method: find seed solution(s) and define linear maps or recurrences preserving the equation (e.g., for x^2+(x+1)^2=y^2, define (x_{n+1},y_{n+1}) = M(x_n,y_n) for integer matrix M). Parametrize Diophantine curves where classical parametrizations exist (Pythagorean triples). Examples: Problem 3.46 (Pythagorean parameterization), Problem 3.47 (linear recurrence that generates infinitely many solutions). Anti-pattern: assuming existence of infinite family without explicit recurrence/parametrization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary representation and powers-of-two reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use binary expansions (number of 1s, sums of powers of two) to deduce structural constraints or impossibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent integers as sums of powers of 2 (e.g., show numbers in sequence can be written as 2^{x_n}+2^{y_n} and track increases of exponents); use popcount constraints to bound ranges with fixed number of 1s in binary. Examples: Problem 3.74 (writing terms as sum of two powers of 2 and tracking exponents), Problems in §3.7. Useful for showing no numbers in an interval can have given binary sparsity. Anti-pattern: ignoring carries/overlaps when summing powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hall's Marriage Lemma (matching condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bipartite matching between n boys and n girls exists iff for every k and every set of k boys, the number of girls acquainted with at least one of them is ≥ k (Hall's condition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use induction on n for the proof; treat cases where every k boys are acquainted with ≥ k+1 girls vs existence of a tight set of k boys with exactly k neighbours. Corollaries: if bipartite graph is m-regular on both sides, a perfect matching exists. Applications: polygon puncturing (areas), selecting one piece per row/column, card-denomination selection, various incidence problems (Problems 3.102–3.111). Anti-pattern: checking only individual degrees rather than Hall's condition for all subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area/measure covering argument to contradict combinatorial bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare total measure (area, count, sum) of a union to covering multiplicities to derive contradictions with assumed small covers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If k unit-area polygons union to area k, they cannot be covered by fewer than k other unit-area polygons — use this to show Hall's condition must hold in polygon overlay problems (Problem 3.102). Similar measure comparisons apply when pieces/weights are conserved. Anti-pattern: ignoring overlaps that change total covered measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting subsequence to convert arithmetic progression into geometric progression
rubrics_metrics.description: From an arithmetic progression of integers, one can remove terms so the remaining terms form a geometric progression by choosing terms of form a(1+r)^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct indices n so that a + (some polynomial in r)·r equals a(1+r)^k; identify a family of terms of arithmetic progression that coincide with successive powers of (1+r) scaled by a. Example: Problem 3.90. Useful when (1+r) multiplies previous term to stay inside the arithmetic list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting fractions in lowest terms to obtain divisor-sum identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Count the fractions i/n (1≤i≤n) in lowest terms by grouping according to denominators (divisors of n) to derive identities involving divisor sums (e.g., sum_{d|n} phi(d)=n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each divisor d of n, count fractions that reduce to denominator d: there are phi(d) of them. Summing over divisors gives n. Example: Problem 3.21. This is a specific application of double counting tailored to multiplicative functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symmetric polynomial/sum identities (e.g., x+y+z=0 ⇒ x^3+y^3+z^3=3xyz)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit classical symmetric identities to factor or simplify algebraic expressions and deduce divisibility/congruence relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize standard symmetric sums and use identities (e.g., if x+y+z=0 then x^3+y^3+z^3=3xyz) to convert sums of cubes into products, enabling factorization or divisibility arguments. Examples: Chapter 4 opening problems (1.4, 1.5) use x+y+z=0 ⇒ sum of cubes = 3xyz and related manipulations. Anti-pattern: applying identity without verifying hypothesis (such as x+y+z=0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity and divisibility chaining arguments in recurrences
rubrics_metrics.description: Track divisibility by primes/powers across terms in a recurrence by induction (showing q divides many terms hence leading to contradiction if constant c >0), often used to force denominators to be 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a rational constant k = p/q occurs in recurrence and q>1, show that q divides later terms iteratively (q^s divides terms after s steps) which may force a contradiction with positivity/smallness of fixed parameters (Problem 3.35). Technique: assume minimal counterexample and propagate divisibility to reach inconsistency. Anti-pattern: neglecting base cases or assuming divisibility without inductive proof.
